title: Persona2Web: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents for Contextual Reasoning with User History
one_liner: Persona2Web tests whether a web agent can use a user's past behavior to resolve ambiguous requests instead of waiting for the user to specify every preference directly.
lead: Real users often ask for something incomplete such as 'book a dinner spot for Friday' or 'find me a laptop for travel' and expect the system to fill in unstated preferences from earlier behavior. Most web-agent benchmarks ignore that problem and reward only direct instruction following. Persona2Web focuses on ambiguous requests plus user history, because personalization is valuable only when the agent can turn past evidence into the missing constraints that make the request concrete.

paras: A request can be syntactically clear yet operationally incomplete. 'Find a hotel for my trip' does not say price range, preferred neighborhood, cancellation habits, or whether the user values quiet rooms over short commutes. Humans expect those gaps to be filled from earlier behavior.

A benchmark that ignores user history cannot reveal whether the agent truly personalizes. It only measures direct task execution after the full preference set is already written into the prompt. That misses the harder part of web assistance: resolving ambiguity from earlier evidence.

callout.html: The agent must infer missing constraints from user history, because many realistic web tasks are underspecified at the moment of request.

steps.text: Give the agent a sequence of past web actions that indirectly reveal stable preferences.
Present a task that cannot be completed well without filling in missing personal context.

steps.b: Let the agent browse and decide
steps.text: The agent uses history plus current web evidence to choose what action to take.

steps.b: Score the chosen action against hidden preferences
steps.text: The benchmark checks whether the agent resolved the missing constraints in a way consistent with the user history.
Evaluation can tell whether the failure came from weak web navigation, weak history use, or weak ambiguity resolution.

paras: The paper changes the benchmark target from plain task completion to personalized task completion under ambiguity. The unit being tested is not just web navigation but contextual preference recovery from history.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: preference evidence strength
hidden.name: preference evidence strength
paras: Preference evidence strength measures how strongly the user history supports one interpretation of the ambiguous request over others. Repeated mid-price bookings and repeated vegetarian choices make one option much more defensible than an expensive steakhouse.

This quantity matters because personalization is not binary. Some histories contain clear repeated patterns, while others are noisy or mixed. A good benchmark must vary that strength so it can test whether agents improve when the history truly contains enough evidence to justify a personalized choice.

heat.caption: Darker means the user history gives stronger evidence for one personalized interpretation.

reads.html: Some histories clearly point to what the user wants, while others only hint at it.
Persona2Web varies user histories and ambiguity levels so evaluation can measure whether agents convert historical preference evidence into correct web choices.

mechanism.h2: Why this benchmark reveals real personalization ability
paras: A direct instruction benchmark cannot distinguish between an agent that understands the user and an agent that simply copies explicit constraints. Persona2Web forces the issue by withholding some of those constraints from the request and placing them in history instead.

The benchmark is informative because the agent must do two linked jobs: interpret history and execute on the live web. If it picks the wrong option despite good browsing, the failure is in preference recovery. If it infers the right preference but cannot act on the website, the failure is in web execution. Separating those pieces makes diagnosis possible.

Using real web tasks matters because personalization is only useful when it changes an actual decision. The benchmark therefore measures whether the recovered preference changes what the agent books, buys, or selects, because that is the point where contextual reasoning becomes user-visible behavior.

stages.s: User history plus a new ambiguous web request
Extract likely personal constraints from repeated past behavior
Combine those constraints with the current web options
Choose and execute the web action that fits both context and page state
Score whether the choice matches the hidden preference implied by history

math.h2: The equation for personalized decision quality
math.words: A decision is good when it satisfies the task request and also matches the preferences implied by the user's history.
symbols: how well the chosen web action satisfies the explicit request
how strongly the evaluation values alignment with user history
how well the chosen option matches the hidden preferences supported by history
overall benchmark score for the agent's final action

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: The request is 'find dinner near the venue.' Two options are equally near.
Option A is vegetarian and mid-price. Option B is steakhouse and expensive.
Suppose both options satisfy the explicit request, so each gets task fit 5.
History shows repeated vegetarian and moderate-price choices, so option A gets preference match 4 and option B gets 0.
With history weight 2, option A scores 5 + 2 * 4 = 13, while option B scores 5 + 2 * 0 = 5.
The benchmark rewards option A because it uses the user's past behavior to resolve the ambiguity.

math.note: The scoring highlights that a task can be completed in a generic way yet still fail as personalized assistance.

charts.title: Generic web agent
charts.note: An agent can browse correctly yet still ignore personal context when the request is underspecified.

charts.title: Personalization-aware agent
charts.note: The gap is largest on ambiguous requests because that is where history provides the missing constraints.

items.html: If the user's past behavior reflects several competing preferences, the benchmark may not have one clear best answer, so evaluation becomes harder to interpret.
Old history can mislead the agent if the user recently changed habits, because repeated past actions no longer describe the current intent.
A strong personalization model can still fail the task if it cannot navigate the website, so the benchmark must separate reasoning failure from browsing failure.
The benchmark is most informative when histories contain interpretable preference traces, ambiguity is controlled, and scoring distinguishes contextual reasoning from web control errors.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a mini shopping or booking website with several equally plausible options under the literal request. Give each synthetic user a history that reveals stable price, cuisine, or location preferences, then ask ambiguous new tasks.

Compare a history-blind agent with a history-aware one. The history-aware agent should choose options that better match the user's past behavior because it uses earlier evidence to fill the missing constraints instead of treating every request as generic.
demo.metric_eq: history_match_rate = history_consistent_choices / ambiguous_tasks and task_completion_rate = completed_tasks / total_tasks
demo.closing: The demo should show that personalization matters most when several options satisfy the explicit request and only the history tells which one the user would actually want.
